newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Regent fund seeks safety in Russia.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Regent fund seeks safety in Russia.

text.p: Peter Everington, investment strategist for the Regent Eastern European Fund, said he's taking a safe route as he begins to buy stocks for the just-launched fund.

Everington said while about 125,000 Russian companies have been privatized, only 200 are actively traded. "We confine our universe to the top 25," said Everington. "We're sticking to what one might call the blue chips first, and keeping our stock risk to as low a level as possible."
Everington, chairman of Regent Fund Management Ltd, the fund's investment advisor, is sticking to utilities, telecommunications, natural resources, and oil and gas issues.

He expects top holdings to include Gazprom, which has a massive amount of natural gas reserves; Rostelekom, the Russian monopoly long distance and international telephone company; and United Energy Systems, which provides all non-nuclear power to Russia and has 120 power stations.
Even these industry monopolies are selling at vast discounts to their real value, Everington argued.
He estimated that oil company reserves in Russia are valued at US$0.10-$0.80 per barrel, dividing market capitalization by the number of barrels.
"Many of the companies we're seeing that go private are vastly undervalued," Everington said. "They have far bigger potential than their initial value."
Everington acknowledges that the fund's name is somewhat of a misnomer as about 35 percent of the 35-40 stocks in the portfolio will be Russian.
The rest of the breakdown is 30 percent in Hungary, 20 percent in Poland, 10 percent in the Czech Republic, and five percent in other countries.
Everington sees great potential in the Ukraine, where privatization is just hitting its stride.
While the fund is capable of buying fixed income securities, Everington expects it to stick primarily with stocks, and a cash position of about five percent.
Everington said that despite economic uncertainties, he is convinced Russia's privatization will land on its feet.

"When Yeltsin came to power, he realized how far behind the economy was, and decided to just throw the entire lot out for privatization," he said. The decision led to abuses and some chaos, but he said it will ultimately lead to stability and prosperity.
He said that other Regent funds have invested a total of about $700 million in Russian securities.
Frank Holmes, chairman of U.S. Global Investors Inc, the fund's sponsor, said he sees the new fund reaching as much as $400 million in assets within two years.
